newsitem.title: POLAND: Suspected arson attack damages Warsaw's synagogue.
newsitem.headline: Suspected arson attack damages Warsaw's synagogue.

text.p: A fire shortly after midnight seriously damaged the vestibule of Warsaw's only working synagogue on Wednesday and both police and leaders of the capital's small Jewish community said they suspected arson.

"I am convinced this is a deliberate act of arson," Rabbi Michael Schudrich told reporters, calling on all Warsaw citizens of good will to come to the building during the evening service, to show solidarity.
"Our initial conclusions show the cause was probably arson," Warsaw police press officer Tomasz Grzelewski said.

"It had to be some inflammable substance thrown in through a window over the entrance," he told Reuters, adding that it was too early to reveal any police theories about who might have been responsible for the attack.
The fire at the central Warsaw Nozyk synagogue was spotted by an employee of a Jewish organisation sleeping in a nearby building and by a policeman posted outside the Jewish theatre.

The fire service quickly put out the blaze which left the large, little used vestibule blackened, with charred debris covering the floor, and destroyed the door but was prevented just in time from spreading to the synagogue's main hall.
One person sleeping in apartments adjoining the synagogue was treated for smoke poisoning, Schudrich and other Jewish community leaders said in a statement.

The statement said that two days before the fire an anonymous telephone caller to the Ronald S. Lauder Foundation, a Jewish educational body nearby, had said "a bomb has been planted or will be planted very soon."
Schudrich, the Lauder foundation representative in Poland, said this was the first such call to the organisation.
Most of Poland's pre-1939 Jewish population of more than three million were murdered by Nazi German invaders during the World War Two Holocaust.

Hundreds of thousands of survivors later emigrated in waves, in part prompted by anti-Semitic episodes such as a 1946 pogrom in the southern city Kielce and an "anti-Zionist" campaign launched by a faction of the then ruling communist party during a power struggle in 1968.
Warsaw, where one third of the pre-war population was Jewish, now has only a few hundred practising Jews.

While there are some tiny extreme-right groups fiercely hostile to minorities, all mainstream Polish political parties condemn anti-Semitism and democratic governments since the 1989 fall of communism have sought to improve ties with the Jewish diaspora and Israel.
But some figures on the fringes of right-leaning parties have made remarks insulting to Jews in recent years -- notably Henryk Jankowski, a priest linked with the Solidarity union.
Jewish community leaders said a failure by these parties and society to condemn such remarks strongly enough might create an atmosphere in which anti-Semitic attacks would be more likely.
"They (remarks) are met with deafening silence," Konstanty Gebert, editor of a Jewish monthly, said outside the synagogue.
A bomb last year smashed windows of Warsaw's kosher restaurant, also near the synagogue, but the motive or exact target of the attack have not so far been explained.
Schudrich called on police to step up patrols of the area around the synagogue, housing key sites of Warsaw Jewish life.
